books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

primary_sources: Florentine Codex, Book 12, c. 1585, public domain

options.text: It killed defenders, including the emperor, and left the city too weak to hold out.
It arrived in the city only after the Aztec Empire had already fallen to the Spanish.
options.misconception: The epidemic struck in late 1520, before the siege, a year before the city fell in 1521.

options.text: It strengthened the Aztec alliance by uniting the subject peoples against the Spanish.
options.misconception: Subject peoples did the opposite: weakened by disease and resentment, many joined the Spanish against Tenochtitlan.

options.text: It affected only the Spanish forces who were besieging the city at the time.
options.misconception: The Spanish had lived with smallpox for centuries and carried some resistance; the epidemic devastated the defenders.

rationales.A: Smallpox spread through Tenochtitlan in late 1520, before the siege, and killed Cuitlahuac, the emperor who had organized the defense after Montezuma's death. With leaders and warriors dying, the city could not hold out against Cortés and his Native allies.
rationales.B: The dates rule this out. The epidemic hit in 1520; Tenochtitlan fell in August 1521, after a siege the disease had already weakened.
rationales.C: Disease pushed subject peoples the other way. Already resentful of Aztec tribute and sacrifice, they saw a weakened empire and joined the Spanish.
rationales.D: The direction is backwards. Spaniards had lived with smallpox for generations; the Mexica had never seen it, so it hit them hardest.
rationales.general:
1. Count the real armies. Cortés brought about 500 men. Smallpox brought something better than men: it arrived in late 1520, months before the siege, and it did not fight fair.
2. Fix the dates. The epidemic struck in late 1520, before the siege; the city fell in 1521.
3. Ask who died. It killed Cuitlahuac, the emperor who had just organized the defense, and the warriors who would have held the causeways.
4. Ask what a siege needs. Defenders, food, and leaders, and the epidemic took all three at once, so the Spanish walked into a city the virus had already beaten.
Remember: in a siege, an epidemic that kills the leaders is worth more than a new weapon.

stem: Smallpox reached Tenochtitlan in late 1520, before Cortés laid siege to the city. What did the epidemic do to the Aztec defense?

stimulus.source_note: Florentine Codex, Book 12, c. 1585, public domain, Wikimedia Commons. Image viewed before writing.
stimulus.text: This drawing from the Florentine Codex, Book 12, shows Nahua people suffering from smallpox in central Mexico in the 1500s. On the left, a sick person covered in spots lies on a mat while another person leans over them. On the right, bodies covered in spots lie still on woven mats, unable to move.
